title: Vue 3: refs, proxies, computed, and timing
outcome: Follow a tracked read and explain why nextTick differs from ordinary assignment.

benefits: Predictable derivation and fewer timing guesses.
drawbacks: Deep and shallow tracking have different contracts.

trace.title: Reactive source
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

reactive returns a proxy. Vue can track property reads through that proxy and notify effects when relevant writes happen. ref creates a reactive value wrapper.

JavaScript uses .value; templates unwrap refs in supported contexts.

computed should calculate a value from tracked sources. Keep it free of network calls and mutations of unrelated state. watch is for a deliberate side effect.

A destructured primitive is no longer a proxy property access; use toRef/toRefs or a getter when a live connection is required.

State assignment happens synchronously, but DOM updates are batched. nextTick waits for Vue’s pending DOM update flush. It does not wait for a network request, image decoding, or every future render.

Measure an element after the relevant update, not by guessing a timeout.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Read query inside computed → Vue records that dependency. Change query → computed becomes stale → a dependent render asks for the new value.

Several synchronous writes can lead to one DOM update batch.

Use shallowRef when you intentionally treat a large outside object as one replaceable value. Deep mutation will not behave like an ordinary deep reactive ref.

Choose it for a reason, such as an external editor instance, not as a universal speed switch.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Watching a computed merely to copy it into another ref creates two sources. Mutating a raw object behind a proxy can bypass the access path you expected Vue to track.
